identity.title: Cross-Entropy Is All You Need To Invert the Data Generating Process

problem.claim: Explain how supervised learning can recover interpretable latent factors and invert aspects of the data-generating process.

gap.claim: A comprehensive theory explaining supervised learning’s effectiveness remains elusive, despite empirical evidence for linear, interpretable representations.

contributions.claim: Extends identifiability results from nonlinear independent component analysis to parametric instance discrimination and supervised cross-entropy minimization.
Proves that, under a specified data-generating process, standard classification models learn ground-truth variation factors up to a linear transformation.
Reports latent-factor recovery across simulated data, the DisLib benchmark, and ImageNet proxy factors.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present a unified theoretical and empirical account connecting cross-entropy-trained supervised representations with inversion of the data-generating process and linear factor representations.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report successful disentanglement on simulated data constructed to match their theoretical assumptions.
The authors report that simple classification tasks on DisLib recover latent structures up to linear transformations.
The authors report that ImageNet-trained models encode representations enabling linear decoding of proxy variation factors.

narrative_sequence.summary: Supervised learning is highly effective, but its effectiveness lacks a comprehensive theory; observed linear representations motivate a latent-factor perspective.
Self-supervised nonlinear independent component analysis provides related evidence that latent structures can be recovered by inverting the data-generating process.
The work extends identifiability results and states a classification result under a particular data-generating process.
Experiments test the account on matched simulations, DisLib, and ImageNet proxy factors.
The authors connect the combined findings to linear-representation observations such as neural-network superposition and to a broader theory of supervised learning.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns a formal representation-identifiability result with empirical checks under matching assumptions, a benchmark, and a real-data proxy-factor setting.

lessons.interpretation: This suggests a useful way to frame theory-driven work: state the scope conditions, then test both assumption-matched behavior and broader empirical correspondences.
lessons.application: For a theory paper, pair each central theorem with an experiment designed around its assumptions, followed by benchmark or real-data probes that test whether the predicted representation property appears beyond the idealized setting.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the contribution is purely conceptual, the theorem has no observable consequence, or no credible proxy for the theoretical object exists.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the exact data-generating-process assumptions, model parameterization, optimization conditions, or formal identifiability statement.
The empirical studies’ sample sizes, metrics, baselines, statistical uncertainty, and whether proxy-factor linear decoding reflects ground-truth factors are not reported.
The abstract does not establish priority, correctness beyond the authors’ reported proof, or independent experimental validity.
